newsitem.title: USA: Bar divided over muni pay-to-play lawyers rule.
newsitem.headline: Bar divided over muni pay-to-play lawyers rule.

text.p: Prominent lawyers attending a volatile American Bar Association (ABA) workshop here espressed deep division over whether ABA should urge law firms nationwide to refrain from "pay-to-play" in municipal bond assignments.
Backers of the strategy said lawyers would be foolish to ignore mounting national concern over influence peddling in the securities and other arenas.
They said action is needed now to head off future legal action by the Securities and Exchange Commission against firms, and that current ABA model rules are inexcusably silent on the issue.
But one opponent accused backers of "bond attorney bashing" and said a rule modeled after a controversial New York City bar standard would be overkill.

Another opponent said existing ABA rules are adequate, that the New York City bar plan would cut lawyers lawyers out of the competitivee political arena and that the plan is dangerous in that it could trigger court sanctions against lawyers.

At the center of the debate is a rule adopted last year by the Association of the Bar of the City of New York that would bar muni bond lawyers that solicit or make contributions to municipal clients, including some PAC contributions, from engaging in bond business for two years with those governments.
The rule is loosely modeled after a standard adopted by the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board in 1994 for muni bond dealers, although the bar's rule is more restrictive.

The New York City bar on March 10 urged the New York State Administrative Board, which sets standards for the state's thousands of lawyers, to adopt the rule for all lawyers in the state. The city bar also wants ABA at its annual meeting in August to urge all state bar groups to adopt the standard.

William Josephson, an official with the New York City bar, told Saturday' workshop that the Administrative Board last week took the first major step toward approval of a rule. He said the Board asked staff to draft a rule for its further consideration.

"We would be foolish to ignore the national concern about political contributions," Josephson said, noting that a New York City bar study shows an "extraordinary correlation" in gift giving between public finance lawyers and influential muni officerholders.
"This isn't some little problem," said New York lawyer and former SEC commissioner Richard Smith at the meeting. "This can't be cured by (improved) disclosure."

This is "something that smells," he said. "Let's get it cleaned up. I don't want (SEC's) foot in the door. I want them to stay out of this area." Smith said while he has problems with parts of the New York City bar's rule, it is a good starting point.

Howard Zucker, a bond lawyer with Hawkins, Delafield & Wood and chairman of a key ABA subpanel, said the city bar's plan is "bond attorney bashing," a "mass of ambiguity" and will lead to "evolutian of as many as 50 different rules" nationwide.
Zucker said pay-to-play is not rampant in the muni bar and that SEC has never done an adequate study of the issue. "The same case against dealers cannot be made against lawyers," he said.

He said a solution may be to amend the SEC's municipal secondary market disclosure rule 15c2-12 to require lawyers to disclose contributions in official statements. "Sunlight would do a world of good," he said.
Lawrence Fox, chairman of ABA's standing committee on ethics and a partner with Drinker Biddle & Reath in Philadelphia, also criticized the New York City bar plan.
"This is very bad policy, bad ethics," he said. ABA already has rules that would cover improper contributions by lawyers, Fox said.
"But they are not working," Paul Maco, head of SEC's Office of Municipal Securities, who also spoke at the workshop, interjected.
Maco said, tongue in cheek, that he is amazed by the "degree of civic interest" some bond lawyers show in contributing to issuers thousands of miles from their voting jurisdictions.

Fox warned that the New York Bar's rule if adopted by ABA could result in sanctions against lawyers. "I view this as a rule that would be adopted by a court, the violation of which would result in a sanction on a lawyer, perhaps disbarment."
--Vicky Stamas, 202-898-8314
